newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - Winter's end for heat.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - Winter's end for heat.

text.p: Mideast Gulf oil product markets could face a shake-up after losses in Singapore kerosene markets on Thursday appeared to close the door on the Asian winter heating fuel season, Gulf traders said.
But Gulf kerosene and gas oil premiums could find some support from a series of buying tenders issued by India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia, they added.
Seasonal weakness in kerosene prices was evident on Thursday with Gulf kerosene giving up most of its 80 cents spread over gas oil on Wednesday. The spread was $2 at the start of March.
Gas oil on Thursday was assessed at $26 a barrel fob Gulf, supported by trade buying in Singapore.
Gulf middle distillate premiums were assessed at 30-50 cents above independent price quotes -- below the $1.00-$1.10 level of last March -- and one kerosene cargo bid was heard at 20 cents.
Arbitrage opportunities that allowed Mediterranean cargoes to compete against Gulf cargoes for Indian sub-continent and Asian demand also added to downward pressure on premiums.
It was left to tenders to provide buying support.
"A combination of term and spot tendering from India and others has kept things interesting," said one trader.

India Oil Corp (IOC) on Thursday issued a tender to buy high speed diesel for delivery in May. This adds to IOC's existing tenders for one-year term supplies of diesel and superior kerosene which closed on March 13.
Pakistan was expected to award a tender for diesel, gasoline and fuel oil imports during April to June in the next 24 hours, traders in the Gulf said.

Bangladesh is in the market for 155,000 barrels of kerosene, Sri Lanka for gasoil and jet fuel and Saudi Arabia for up to 1.5 million barrels of gasoline to meet transport fuel demands related to next month's annual haj pilgrimage, traders said.

Details on any award of gasoline by Saudi Aramco were slow to emerge from the market though traders said that current high premiums for gasoline would make Aramco cut its purchases to around one million barrels.
"Aramco is probably trying its very best to keep imports down to a minimum given the state of premiums," said a trader.
